title: Abdic's Rebellion: The Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia
sources: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), Bihac pocket findings
content:
Fikret Abdić was, by nearly any measure, the most popular politician in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the November 1990 elections, he received more individual votes than any other candidate for the Bosnian presidency, including Alija Izetbegović, who nonetheless assumed the rotating chairmanship by party agreement. Abdić was a self-made businessman from the Cazinska Krajina — the far northwestern corner of Bosnia centered on Velika Kladuša — where he had built the Agrokomerc conglomerate into a regional economic powerhouse before its spectacular financial collapse in 1987. His local following was immense, rooted less in ideology than in patronage and a fierce regional identity that sat uneasily with Sarajevo's authority.

By mid-1993, the Bihać pocket was in desperate condition. Cut off from the rest of government-held territory and surrounded by Bosnian Serb and Croatian Serb forces, the pocket's population endured severe shortages of food, medicine, and military supplies. The ARBiH 5th Corps under General Atif Dudaković defended the enclave with tenacity, but the siege created internal fractures. Abdić, who had maintained informal contacts with both Serbian and Croatian interlocutors throughout the war, grew increasingly critical of Izetbegović's rejection of the Owen-Stoltenberg peace plan, which Abdić believed offered the best available terms for ending the war.

On 27 September 1993, Abdić declared the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia, with its seat in Velika Kladuša. The declaration represented the most serious internal rupture within Bosniak political and military structures during the entire conflict. Abdić framed his action as a pragmatic response to Sarajevo's intransigence — a local leader choosing peace and economic survival over a war he considered unwinnable on Izetbegović's terms. His supporters in the Cazinska Krajina, numbering in the tens of thousands, rallied behind him.

The consequences were immediate and strategically profound. Abdić formed armed units that entered into open alliance with the VRS and, at various points, with Croatian Serb forces from the RSK. The 5th Corps, already stretched thin against external siege, now faced a second front within the pocket itself. Fighting between forces loyal to Abdić and those loyal to the Sarajevo government produced significant casualties and displaced tens of thousands of civilians within an area already suffering acute humanitarian crisis.

The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) addressed the Bihać pocket extensively, documenting how VRS strategy in northwestern Bosnia exploited the Abdić split to maintain pressure on the enclave. The alliance between Abdić's forces and the VRS was not merely tactical convenience — it reflected a calculated Bosnian Serb interest in keeping the pocket divided and weak.

Abdić's rebellion defies simple characterization. To his followers, he was a leader who prioritized their survival over distant Sarajevo's political calculations. To the Bosnian government, he was a traitor who fractured the defense of the most vulnerable enclave at its most critical hour. The fighting within the Bihać pocket between 1993 and 1995 — Bosniaks killing Bosniaks while surrounded by hostile forces — stands as one of the war's most tragic chapters, a conflict within a conflict that compounded the suffering of a population already enduring siege conditions.
